items: Open **Topic 1.1 Moles and Molar Mass** in **Guided** mode. Use **Next** to move through the 6 steps.
Leave **Substance** on **H₂O (Water)** (starts at **18.0 g**). The mass control works only on step 6 and in Free Explore; a new substance resets the mass to one molar mass.

items.prompt: If you double the mass of water, what happens to the moles and the number of molecules?
items.answer: Both double. For the same substance, moles and particles change in proportion to the mass.

items: n = {{moles|10}}   N = {{particles|10}}   m = {{mass|8}}   M = {{molar mass|12}}
We measure {{mass}}, then use the {{mole}} to connect mass to amount of substance.
The {{molar mass}} tells how many grams correspond to {{one}} mole of the substance.
To find moles, {{divide}} the sample mass by the {{molar mass}}.
One mole always contains {{6.022 × 10²³}} particles (Avogadro's number). Ionic NaCl is counted in {{formula units}}, not molecules.
Each conversion factor {{cancels}} the previous unit until only the desired unit remains.

items.prompt: Do this BEFORE you click to step 3: how many moles are in the 18.0 g H₂O sample?
items.answer: n = m / M = 18.0 g ÷ 18.0 g/mol = **1.00 mol** H₂O (step 3 shows 1.00 mol).

items.prompt: BEFORE step 6: find the moles and formula units in 36.0 g NaCl (M = 58.4 g/mol), to 3 sig. figs.
items.answer: n = 36.0 g ÷ 58.4 g/mol = 0.616 mol (sim shows 0.62 mol). N = 0.616 mol × 6.022 × 10²³ = **3.71 × 10²³ formula units** (sim: 3.71 × 10²³).

blocks.title: Data table: Step 6 / Free Explore
blocks.subtitle: Row 1: starting mass. Row 2: slide to the top of the scale. Row 3: click NaCl, type 36.0 in the Mass box

items.prompt: 36.0 g of H₂O and 36.0 g of NaCl have the same mass. Which sample has more particles? Use your data and molar mass to explain.
items.answer: H₂O: 1.203 × 10²⁴ molecules vs. 3.71 × 10²³ formula units of NaCl. Water's molar mass (18.0 g/mol) is smaller than NaCl's (58.4 g/mol), so each gram holds more moles and more particles. Accept: smaller molar mass → more moles per gram.

items: Open **Topic 1.2 Mass Spectra of Elements** in **Guided** mode. Steps 1–5 always use **neon (Ne)** at natural abundance.

On step 6, the **Element** buttons (Neon, Magnesium, Boron, Silicon) and the **Abundance Controls** sliders turn on. Moving one slider changes the others so the total stays 100%; clicking an element resets natural abundances.

items.prompt: Neon has isotopes with mass numbers 20, 21 and 22. Neon's atomic mass is about 20.18. Which isotope do you predict is the most abundant? Why?
items.answer: Neon-20, because the average (20.18) is very close to 20. Accept any answer that uses the average being near 20.

items: Relative abundance = {{amount of one isotope ÷ total amount|32}} × 100
Average atomic mass = Σ ( {{isotope mass × fractional abundance|34}} )
The sample contains only neon, but its atoms do not all have the same {{mass}}. These different masses come from {{isotopes}}.
Each isotope appears at a different {{m/z}} value because each isotope has a different mass.
The tallest peak is the {{most abundant}} isotope, not the heaviest. Peak height tracks {{abundance}}.
Periodic-table atomic mass is a {{weighted average}} of isotope masses, so it is usually not a whole number.

items.prompt: BEFORE step 5: with masses 19.992, 20.994, 21.991 amu, calculate neon's average atomic mass.
BEFORE you click Boron: ¹⁰B 10.013 amu (19.9%), ¹¹B 11.009 amu (80.1%). Calculate the average.

blocks.title: Data table: Step 6 natural abundance
blocks.subtitle: Click each element button and record the Isotope Data panel

items.prompt: On step 6 (Boron), drag the sliders until the two peaks are about the same height. What average atomic mass does the sim show? Explain why.
items.answer: About 10.51 amu, halfway between 10.013 and 11.009, because equal abundances give each isotope equal weight. Accept 10.4–10.6 amu with the equal-weight reasoning.

items: Open **Topic 1.3 Elemental Composition of Pure Substances** in **Guided** mode. Keep the toggle on **Molecular** (the example compound: C 40.0 g, H 6.7 g, O 53.3 g).
**Do not move the Sample mass slider.** Keep it at **100.0 g**. (The sim rounds each element to 0.1 g every time the slider moves, so the percentages drift.)
If the slider was moved, click **Formula unit**, then **Molecular**, to reset the example.

items.prompt: A 50 g sample and a 100 g sample of the same pure compound: will the percent by mass of carbon be different? Why?
items.answer: No. A pure compound has a fixed composition by mass (law of definite proportions), so % C is the same for any sample size.

items: % by mass = {{mass of element ÷ total mass of compound|36}} × 100
mass of element = {{% ÷ 100|10}} × total sample mass      n = {{m ÷ M|8}}
ratio = {{moles of each element ÷ smallest mole value|38}}
multiplier = {{molecular molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass|38}}
A pure compound has a fixed {{mass composition}}. This is the law of {{definite proportions}}.
A {{100.0 g}} sample makes each percent value read directly as grams.
Masses do not directly give atom counts. Convert grams to {{moles}} so the elements can be compared by amount.
Divide every mole amount by the {{smallest}} mole amount.
Empirical formula = {{lowest whole-number}} ratio of atoms.
For a molecular compound, compare {{molecular molar mass}} with empirical-formula mass to find the multiplier.
Ionic compounds stay as {{formula units}}; they are not scaled into molecules.

items.prompt: Do this BEFORE step 5: glucose has empirical formula CH₂O and molar mass 180.16 g/mol. Find the empirical formula mass, the multiplier and the molecular formula.
Click **Formula unit**: Mg 60.3 g and O 39.7 g. Calculate the moles of each and the empirical formula. Then check the sim.
A student says the mass data C 40.0 g, H 6.7 g, O 53.3 g means the formula is C₄₀H₇O₅₃. Use the sim's steps to explain the mistake.
items.answer: Masses do not give atom counts. You must divide each mass by its atomic mass to get moles (3.33, 6.65, 3.33), then divide by the smallest (1 : 2 : 1), giving CH₂O.

items: Open **Topic 1.4 Composition of Mixtures** in **Guided** mode. It starts with **CO 14.0 g**; from step 2, **CO₂ 22.0 g** is added (the “50-50 mol example”).
Leave both sliders at these values for steps 1–5. This topic uses **C = 12** and **O = 16** g/mol exactly. On step 6, use the preset buttons: **50-50 mol example, Pure CO, Pure CO₂, Mystery sample**.

items.prompt: When CO₂ is mixed into pure CO, will the percent oxygen of the sample go up, go down or stay the same? Why?
items.answer: Go up, because CO₂ has a higher percent oxygen than CO (72.7% vs. 57.1%).

items: m(element) = {{mass of substance|16}} × {{element mass ÷ molar mass|24}}
% composition = {{mass of element ÷ total mass|28}} × 100
Step 1 has one kind of molecule, {{carbon monoxide}}: a pure substance with a fixed {{composition}} by mass.
Adding CO₂ makes a {{mixture}} (two particle types); the relative amounts can {{vary}}.
When the mass of carbon stays the same, CO₂ has {{twice}} as much oxygen as CO: {{32}} g O vs. 16 g O per 12 g C. This shows the Law of {{Multiple Proportions}}.
A mixture gives an {{intermediate}} composition between the pure CO and pure CO₂ endpoints.

items.prompt: BEFORE step 4: calculate % C and % O of the whole mixture.
BEFORE step 5: f(CO₂) = (%O sample − 57.1) ÷ (72.7 − 57.1). Find the CO₂ mass fraction.

blocks.title: Data table: Step 6 presets
blocks.subtitle: Click each preset; read the Live Chart and the Analysis Workspace

items.prompt: Is the mystery sample pure or a mixture? Give a claim and use its % O as evidence.
items.answer: Mixture. Its 68.8% O is between pure CO (57.1%) and pure CO₂ (72.7%), so it cannot be either pure compound. It is about 75% CO₂ by mass.

items: Open **Topic 1.5 Atomic Structure and Electron Configuration** in **Guided** mode. It starts on **chlorine (Cl, Z = 17)**, neutral.
Step 2 has two sliders: **Electron shell distance** (n = 1 to 3) and **Nuclear charge for comparison**. Moving the nuclear-charge slider changes the atom, so put it back on **17 (Cl)** before step 3.
Steps 3–5 use the **Atom identity** slider; step 5 adds charge buttons (for example Cl⁻).
Z = {{number of protons|18}}      Neutral atom: e⁻ = {{p⁺|6}}
Nucleus = {{protons + neutrons|20}}      F(Coulombic) ∝ {{q₁q₂ ÷ r²|10}}
The element is defined by its {{proton}} count. A neutral atom has the same number of {{electrons}} as protons.
Opposite charges {{attract}}. Electrons {{closer}} to a positive nucleus feel a stronger pull.
Shells are broad energy levels. {{Subshells}} divide those shells into smaller regions with fixed capacities.
The Aufbau principle says electrons fill the {{lowest}} available energy subshells first.
Capacities: s = {{2}}, p = {{6}}, d = {{10}}, f = {{14}} electrons.
The {{superscript}} on each subshell tells how many electrons were placed there.
Core electrons are {{inner}} electrons. Valence electrons are in the {{highest occupied}} shell.
Ion formation changes the {{electron}} count, but the {{proton}} count in the nucleus stays the same.

blocks.title: Data table: Step 2 Coulomb attraction (Cl, Z = 17)

items.prompt: Do this BEFORE step 4: fill 17 electrons into 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p in order. Write chlorine's configuration.

blocks.title: Data table: Steps 4–6
blocks.subtitle: Use the Atom identity slider and charge buttons; read the atom model and Electron Summary

items.prompt: Use your step 2 data and Coulomb's law to explain why chlorine's n = 3 electrons are held less strongly than its n = 1 electrons.
items.answer: Same nuclear charge (17), but n = 3 electrons are farther away (larger r). Force ∝ q₁q₂/r², so the pull drops from 17.00 (n = 1) to 1.89 (n = 3). Accept: greater distance → weaker attraction.

items: Open **Topic 1.6 Photoelectron Spectroscopy** in **Guided** mode. It starts on **neutral sodium (Na)**. Click a peak to select it. The axis is **relative**: peaks are evenly spaced, so compare order, not distances.

The **Species** buttons (Na, Na⁺, Mg, Mg²⁺, Al, Ne) are always on screen: keep **Na** for steps 1–4. Step 5 adds **Na (neutral) / Na⁺ (positive ion)** buttons; step 6 adds a **single / overlay** toggle.

items.prompt: Sodium is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹. Predict how many PES peaks it has and which peak is tallest.
items.answer: 4 peaks (one per occupied subshell: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s). The 2p peak is tallest (6 electrons).

items: atom + hν → ion + {{e⁻|6}}          peak height ∝ {{number of electrons|20}}
Binding energy = {{energy required to remove an electron|36}}
PES removes electrons from atoms and measures the {{energy pattern}} that comes back.
A PES spectrum gives a peak for each occupied {{subshell}}, not one peak for each shell.
Peak {{height}} is proportional to the number of electrons in that subshell.
Peak {{position}} shows binding energy: the energy required to {{remove}} an electron.
When sodium forms a positive ion, the outer {{3s}} electron is removed. The remaining electrons feel less {{shielding}}, so their peaks shift to {{higher}} binding energy.

blocks.prompt: Sketch the Na spectrum from step 3. Put higher binding energy on the LEFT, as the sim does. Label each peak.
blocks.answer: Left to right: 1s (2), 2s (2), 2p (tallest, 6), 3s (smallest, 1). Shape and order only.

blocks.title: Data table: Steps 5–6 (Species buttons)
blocks.subtitle: Record the Live Summary for each species

items.prompt: Why is the 2p peak taller than the 2s peak? Why is the 1s peak at the highest binding energy?
items.answer: Height ∝ electrons: 2p has 6, 2s has 2. 1s electrons are closest to the nucleus and least shielded, so removal takes the most energy.

items.prompt: Why does Na⁺ lose the 3s peak, and what happens to the remaining peaks? (Step 5 shows “Ion shift”.)
items.answer: Na⁺ has lost its only 3s electron, so the 3s peak disappears. The rest feel less shielding, so all 3 peaks shift to higher binding energy (“3 peaks higher”).

items: Open **Topic 1.7 Periodic Trends** in **Guided** mode. Path: **Across Period 3** (other buttons: **Down Group 1**, **Down Group 17**).

On step 1, click an element button to make it active; the **Property preview** shows its radius, first ionization energy and electronegativity. Step 3 has **Atom / Cation / Anion** tabs. Step 5 has an **Electron affinity / Electronegativity** toggle.

items.prompt: Rank Na, Mg and Cl from largest to smallest atomic radius. Give one reason.
items.answer: Na > Mg > Cl. Same number of shells, but more protons (higher Zeff) pull the electrons closer across the period.

items: Zeff ≈ {{Z − S|8}}   (S = core-electron shielding)
First ionization: M(g) → M⁺(g) + {{e⁻|6}}    Electron affinity: X(g) + e⁻ → {{X⁻(g)|8}}
Across a period, protons {{increase}} while the main shielding shell stays similar, so Zeff usually {{increases}}.
Across a period, higher Zeff pulls the same main shell {{closer}}, so atoms usually get {{smaller}}.
Down a group, new shells and more distance usually dominate, so atoms get {{bigger}}. Cations {{shrink}}; anions {{expand}}.
First ionization energy is the energy needed to {{remove}} the first electron from a neutral atom.
Electron affinity describes attracting an added {{electron}}. Electronegativity describes pulling shared electrons in a {{bond}}.
Both become {{stronger}} when Zeff is high and the attracted electron is close to the nucleus.

blocks.title: Data table: Period 3 (steps 1, 4 and 5)
blocks.subtitle: Radius, ionization energy and electronegativity from step 1; electron affinity from step 5

blocks.title: Data table: Step 3 Atom / Cation / Anion tabs

items.prompt: Na (190 pm) is much larger than Cl (79 pm) even though Cl has more electrons. Explain with Zeff and shells.
items.answer: Both have 3 occupied shells and the same 10 core electrons, but Cl's Zeff (7) is much higher than Na's (1), so Cl pulls its valence shell much closer.

items.prompt: First IE generally increases across Period 3, but Mg (738) > Al (578) and P (1012) > S (1000). Which electron is removed in Al? Suggest why it is easier to remove.
items.answer: Al loses a 3p electron; it is higher in energy and partly shielded by the 3s² electrons, so it is easier to remove than Mg's 3s electron. (For S, the paired 3p electron repels its partner.) The sim shows these values but does not explain them; accept either reason with evidence.

items: Open **Topic 1.8 Valence Electrons and Ionic Compounds** in **Guided** mode (starts with **Na** and **Cl**). From step 2, choose a **Metal** (Li, Na, K, Mg, Ca, Al) and a **Nonmetal** (F, Cl, Br, O, S, N, P). Al with Cl or Br is greyed out.
Step 5 has **Change metal / Change nonmetal**. Step 6 has **Shells / Charges / Formula / Trends** views.

items.prompt: Predict the formula of the compound of magnesium and chlorine. Explain using valence electrons.
items.answer: MgCl₂: Mg has 2 valence electrons and loses them (Mg²⁺); each Cl gains 1 (Cl⁻), so two Cl⁻ balance one Mg²⁺.

items: (cations × cation charge) + (anions × anion charge) = {{0|6}}
Periodic table position predicts the {{outer}} electrons that control {{reactivity}}.
Bonding starts with {{attraction}} between valence electrons and {{nuclei}}.
Metals on the {{left}} usually reach stability by {{losing}} valence electrons. Nonmetals on the {{right}} usually reach stability by {{gaining}} electrons.
Losing electrons makes a {{positive}} ion. Gaining electrons makes a {{negative}} ion.
Ionic compounds are {{neutral}} overall, so total positive charge must {{equal}} total negative charge.
The {{formula}} records the smallest whole-number ion ratio.
Elements in the same column have related {{valence}} patterns, which produce analogous ionic compounds.

items.prompt: BEFORE you build it: Al forms Al³⁺ and O forms O²⁻. Find the ion ratio, formula, and electrons moved per formula unit.
items.answer: LCM of 3 and 2 is 6: 2 Al³⁺ (+6) and 3 O²⁻ (−6). Ratio 2 : 3, **Al₂O₃**; 2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0. **6 electrons** move (sim: “Transferred 6”).

items.prompt: Step 5, Change metal, with Cl: the sim lists LiCl, NaCl and KCl. Why do they all have the same 1 : 1 pattern?
items.answer: Li, Na and K are all in Group 1 with 1 valence electron, so each forms a 1+ ion that balances one Cl⁻.

items.prompt: The sim names K as the most reactive Group 1 metal. Use its first ionization energy and atomic structure to justify this.
items.answer: K has the lowest first IE in the group (419 kJ/mol vs. 496 for Na and 520 for Li) because its valence electron is in the 4th shell, farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost most easily.

conclusion.prompt: Topics 1.5–1.7: why is Na's 3s PES peak lowest in energy, its radius large and its first IE low?
conclusion.answer: 3s is far out (n = 3) and shielded (Zeff ≈ 1): weak pull → lowest PES peak, 190 pm radius, IE 496 kJ/mol.

conclusion.prompt: Topics 1.5 and 1.8: why Mg²⁺ (not Mg⁺ or Mg³⁺), and why MgCl₂?
conclusion.answer: Losing both 3s electrons leaves a full shell; a 3rd would be a core electron. 2 Cl⁻ balance Mg²⁺: MgCl₂.

key_notes: **Topic 1.1:** molar masses use the sim's atomic masses (H 1.008, C 12.011, O 15.999, Na 22.99, Cl 35.45; domain/chemistry/periodic-table.ts). The screen rounds molar mass to 0.1 g/mol, but the sim divides by the unrounded value. So 36.0 g H₂O shows 2.00 mol but 1.203 × 10²⁴ molecules (2.00 × 6.022 × 10²³ would give 1.204). Accept 1.20 × 10²⁴ (3 significant figures).

**Topic 1.1:** the starting mass of each substance is exactly one molar mass (18.015 g for H₂O, shown as 18.0 g). The mass box, the − / + buttons (±1.0 g) and the scale only work on step 6 and in Free Explore. The H₂O scale runs 0–36.0 g.

**Topic 1.2:** isotope data: ²⁰Ne 19.992 amu 90.48%, ²¹Ne 20.994 0.27%, ²²Ne 21.991 9.25%; Mg 23.985/24.986/25.983 at 78.99/10.0/11.01%; B 10.013/11.009 at 19.9/80.1%; Si 27.977/28.976/29.974 at 92.23/4.67/3.1% (domain/chemistry/isotopes.ts:8-28). The sim shows abundance to 0.1% (90.5, 0.3, 9.3) and fractions to 4 places. Si's average shows 28.086 (the periodic table in the sim uses 28.085).

**Topic 1.3:** do NOT let students drag or type in the Sample mass control on steps 2–4. Each move rescales and rounds every element to 0.1 g, and the errors pile up: dragging 100 → 50 g gives H 5.0% and formula CHO; dragging 100 → 200 g gives CH₃O. Reset by clicking Formula unit, then Molecular. Glucose molar mass is fixed at 180.16 g/mol in the sim.

**Topic 1.4** uses C = 12 and O = 16 exactly (calculations.ts:95-98), unlike the other topics (12.011, 15.999). So M(CO) = 28.00 and M(CO₂) = 44.00 g/mol. Pure CO: 42.9% C / 57.1% O; pure CO₂: 27.3% C / 72.7% O. The CO₂ fraction is computed from unrounded percents (0.611); students using rounded percents get 0.615.

**Topic 1.5:** the step 2 “relative pull” is the sim's model Z ÷ n² (17.00, 4.25, 1.89 for Cl), not a measured force; the worksheet asks only for the values shown. Neutrons are the rounded atomic mass minus Z (Cl: 35 − 17 = 18). The sim counts all electrons in the highest occupied shell as valence, so it reports Mg²⁺ as 8 valence electrons; many textbooks would say Mg²⁺ has none. Cl's charge buttons include +1, +5 and +7 (oxidation states, not simple ions).

**Topic 1.6:** binding energies are a model (Z ÷ n² + a small subshell offset; ions scaled up 10% per + charge), labelled “relative.” Do not use them as real values (real Na: 1s ≈ 104, 3s ≈ 0.50 MJ/mol). Peaks are evenly spaced, and in overlay mode the ion's peaks are drawn in the same place as the atom's, so students see the shift only in the “Ion shift: 3 peaks higher” readout. The worksheet asks only for order and height.

**Topic 1.7:** atomic radii are the sim's values (Na 190, Mg 145, Al 118, Si 111, P 98, S 88, Cl 79, Ar 71, Li 167, K 243 pm), which are calculated radii and are larger for metals than many textbook tables (e.g. Na 186 pm). Ionic radii: Na⁺ 102, Mg²⁺ 72, Al³⁺ 54, Cl⁻ 181, S²⁻ 184, P³⁻ 212, Li⁺ 76, K⁺ 138, F⁻ 133, Br⁻ 196 pm. EA is shown as a positive number (energy released) and Mg, N and Ar show 0. Ar's electronegativity shows “0” on step 5 (it has no value). The sim's Zeff = Z − core electrons (so Zeff = number of valence electrons).

**Topic 1.8:** charges come from each element's first common ion (N³⁻, P³⁻, O²⁻, S²⁻). Al–Cl and Al–Br are blocked on purpose (state.ts:27). “Most reactive metal” = lowest first IE in the group; “strongest nonmetal attraction” = highest electronegativity. The pattern line reads “Group 1 metals repeat a + charge pattern” (the 1 is missing); say “1+”.

Settings that change answers: the substance (1.1), the element and slider positions (1.2), the Sample mass slider (1.3), the mass sliders and presets (1.4), the nuclear-charge slider (1.5, it changes the atom), the species button (1.6), the path, radius tab and property toggle (1.7), and the metal/nonmetal pair (1.8).

lesson_plan.sim_location: chemsims.app/sims/unit1 → Unit 1 Atomic Structure and Properties → Topics 1.1–1.8 (each has Guided mode and Free Explore)
lesson_plan.essential_question: How do the masses, counts and arrangement of particles in atoms explain the composition of substances, the periodic trends and the formulas of ionic compounds?
objectives: Convert between mass, moles and particles with n = m/M and N = n × Nₐ (1.1).
Read a mass spectrum and calculate an average atomic mass as a weighted average (1.2).
Find an empirical formula from mass data and a molecular formula from molar mass (1.3).
Use elemental composition to decide whether a sample is pure or a mixture (1.4).
Write ground-state electron configurations and relate them to Coulomb attraction (1.5).
Interpret PES peak height and position, including for ions (1.6).
Explain atomic radius, ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity trends with Zeff and shells (1.7).
Predict ion charges and ionic formulas from valence electrons (1.8).
materials: A periodic table for each student (for checking, not for blanks)
prep: Run Topic 1.1 Guided once on the projector; the sim opens full screen. Know where Next, the Substance buttons and the step-6 mass box are.
Open Topic 1.3 and practise the reset: Formula unit → Molecular. Warn students not to move the Sample mass slider.
Read the Answer Key's Teacher Notes page (sim values that differ from textbooks).

The sim doesn't cover orbital diagrams/Hund's rule, transition-metal configurations and ions (4s removed first), real PES energies in MJ/mol, or combustion/experimental empirical-formula analysis; use your usual lesson for these.
prior_knowledge: Protons, neutrons and electrons and their charges
Reading the periodic table (groups and periods)

days.title: Teacher demo: Moles and Molar Mass (Topic 1.1)
days.goal: Students see how the sim works and connect mass → moles → particles.
agenda: Warm-up: “How would you count the molecules in a glass of water?”
Hand out packets. Students fill the 1.1 Set Up and Predict boxes.
Projected demo of Topic 1.1 steps 1–6 (script below).
Students finish the 1.1 Guided notes and equations with a partner.
Quick check: “How many moles in 36.0 g of water?” (2.00 mol)

demo_script.do: Open chemsims.app/sims/unit1, choose Topic 1.1 Moles and Molar Mass, Guided mode. Point to the four panels: Sample, Conversion Pathway, Measurements, Equation and Working.
demo_script.say: “We can't count atoms one at a time. What CAN we measure in the lab?” (Expected: mass.)
demo_script.students: Set Up box; Predict: doubling the mass doubles moles and molecules.

demo_script.do: Step 1 “Why do we use the mole?”: point to the balance (18.0 g H₂O) and the grey Molar Mass, Moles and Particles boxes.
demo_script.say: “Only mass is lit up. The mole is the bridge from mass to amount.”
demo_script.students: First notes line: measure mass, use the mole.

demo_script.do: Point to the muted equations: n = m/M, N = n × Nₐ, Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
demo_script.say: “What does each letter stand for?” (n moles, m mass, M molar mass, N particles.)

demo_script.do: Click Next → step 2 “Building the molar mass”. Show the molecule view (2 H atoms, 1 O atom) and “2 x 1.0 + 16.0 = 18.0 g mol⁻¹”.
demo_script.say: “Why do we multiply hydrogen by 2?” (Two H atoms in each molecule.) “What does 18.0 g/mol mean?” (One mole of water has a mass of 18.0 g.)
demo_script.students: Step 2 data table; molar mass notes line; amu ↔ grams line.

demo_script.do: Do NOT click Next yet. Give 1 minute for Calculate #1.
demo_script.say: “How many moles are in 18.0 g of water? Show the units cancelling.”

demo_script.do: Click Next → step 3. Point to Moles: 1.00 mol and the note “The grams cancel, leaving moles.”
demo_script.say: “Did your answer match? Which unit cancelled?” (grams)
demo_script.students: Notes: divide the sample mass by the molar mass.

demo_script.do: Click Next → step 4. Read “1.00 mol × 6.022 × 10²³ = 6.022 × 10²³ molecules.”
demo_script.say: “How many molecules would 2 moles hold?” (1.204 × 10²⁴.) “Is a mole a mass or a number?” (a number)
demo_script.students: Notes: one mole always contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles.

demo_script.do: Click Next → step 5. Trace the dimensional-analysis chain left to right.
demo_script.say: “Each factor cancels the unit before it. What is left at the end?” (molecules)
demo_script.students: Notes: each factor cancels the previous unit.

demo_script.do: Click Next → step 6. Drag the H₂O mass scale to the right end (36.0 g).
demo_script.say: “Check your prediction. What happened to moles and particles?” (2.00 mol, 1.203 × 10²⁴ — both doubled. The last digit is 1.203, not 1.204, because the sim uses 18.015 g/mol.)

demo_script.do: Click NaCl. Point out that the mass jumps to 58.4 g (one molar mass) and the particles are “formula units”.
demo_script.say: “Why not molecules?” (NaCl is ionic, no separate molecules.) Stop here: students do the rest on Day 2.
demo_script.students: Notes: ionic NaCl is counted in formula units.

days.title: Student sim work: Topics 1.4–1.5
days.goal: Use composition to judge purity; build electron configurations.
agenda: Warm-up: “What is the difference between a compound and a mixture?”

days.title: Grading and wrap-up
days.goal: Students check their work, correct errors and review misconceptions.
agenda: Grading (self, peer or teacher; see the grading section).
Discussion: the misconceptions below; students explain one correction to the class.
Exit ticket.

misconceptions.misconception: The tallest peak in a mass spectrum is the heaviest isotope.
misconceptions.sim_fix: Topic 1.2 step 3 says “The tallest peak is not the heaviest isotope. It is the most abundant isotope.” Show ²⁰Ne (90.5%) vs ²²Ne (9.3%).

misconceptions.misconception: Mass percents can be used directly as subscripts (C₄₀H₇O₅₃).
misconceptions.sim_fix: Topic 1.3 step 3: “Masses do not directly give atom counts.” Students see 40.0 g C become 3.33 mol.

misconceptions.misconception: Equal masses mean equal numbers of particles.
misconceptions.sim_fix: Topic 1.1 step 6: 36.0 g H₂O has 1.203 × 10²⁴ molecules but 36.0 g NaCl has only 3.71 × 10²³ formula units.

misconceptions.misconception: PES shows one peak per shell.
misconceptions.sim_fix: Topic 1.6 step 2: sodium has separate 2s and 2p peaks, so 4 peaks for 3 shells.

misconceptions.misconception: Atoms with more electrons are always bigger.
misconceptions.sim_fix: Topic 1.7: Cl (17 electrons) is 79 pm but Na (11 electrons) is 190 pm; Zeff 7 vs 1.

sim_cautions: Topic 1.3: tell students not to move the Sample mass slider. The sim rounds every element mass each time it moves, so the percentages drift and the formula can change (CHO or CH₃O). To fix it, click Formula unit, then Molecular.
Topic 1.1: the sim divides by the unrounded molar mass (18.015), so 36.0 g of water shows 2.00 mol but 1.203 × 10²⁴ molecules, not 1.204. Both are right to 3 significant figures.
Topic 1.4 uses C = 12 and O = 16 exactly, but the other topics use 12.011 and 15.999. Tell students to use the numbers on that screen.

Topic 1.6: the binding energies are model numbers, not real ones, and the peaks are evenly spaced. In overlay mode the ion's peaks sit on top of the atom's; the shift to higher energy is only in the “Ion shift” readout.
Topic 1.5 step 2: the “Nuclear charge for comparison” slider changes the element. Put it back on 17 for chlorine.
Topic 1.5: the sim counts Mg²⁺'s eight n = 2 electrons as “valence electrons.” Tell students many textbooks say a cation like Mg²⁺ has a noble-gas core and no valence electrons left.
Topic 1.7 step 5: argon shows an electronegativity of “0”. That means there is no value, not that it is zero. Mg and Ar also show an electron affinity of 0.
Topic 1.8: the pattern line says “repeat a + charge pattern” for Group 1; read it as “1+”.
Topic 1.3 Free Explore: the first Try-it says to change the sample mass, but Free Explore only has element mass boxes. Have students double every element mass instead.

support: Pair students; one drives the sim, the other records, then swap each topic.
Give a blank Aufbau order strip (1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s) for Topic 1.5.
For calculations, provide the formula with blanks for the numbers.
Allow students to finish one Free Explore item instead of the full Explore box.
extension: 1.2: set ²⁴Mg, ²⁵Mg and ²⁶Mg to one-third each and predict the average first.
1.4: find the CO and CO₂ masses that give exactly 65.0% O.
1.7: explain why F's electron affinity (328) is lower than Cl's (349).
1.8: predict the formulas of all Group 2 + Group 15 compounds and check them in Free Explore.

exit_ticket.question: How many moles and molecules are in 9.0 g of water (M = 18.0 g/mol)?
Boron is 19.9% ¹⁰B (10.013 amu) and 80.1% ¹¹B (11.009 amu). Which peak is taller, and what is the average atomic mass?
exit_ticket.answer: ¹¹B is taller (more abundant); average = 10.811 amu.

exit_ticket.question: Write the formula for the compound of calcium and nitrogen and show the charge balance.

ap_practice.question: Multiple choice. Na and Mg²⁺ have PES spectra. Which is true? (A) Mg²⁺ has a 3s peak. (B) Both have a 2p peak with height 6, but Mg²⁺ has one fewer peak. (C) Na has fewer peaks than Mg²⁺. (D) The 1s peak of Na is at a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of Mg²⁺.
ap_practice.answer: (B). Na: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s (4 peaks); Mg²⁺: 1s, 2s, 2p (3 peaks); both 2p⁶. Mg²⁺ has more protons (12 vs 11) and fewer electrons, so its 1s binding energy is higher, which rules out (D).

ap_practice.question: FRQ. A 100.0 g sample of a compound contains 40.0 g C, 6.7 g H and 53.3 g O. (a) Find the moles of each element. (b) Find the empirical formula. (c) The molar mass is 180.16 g/mol; find the molecular formula. (d) A second 50.0 g sample of the same compound is analyzed. Predict its percent by mass of carbon and name the law that justifies your answer.
ap_practice.answer: (a) C 40.0/12.011 = 3.33 mol; H 6.7/1.008 = 6.65 mol; O 53.3/15.999 = 3.33 mol. (b) ÷ 3.33 → 1 : 2 : 1, CH₂O. (c) 180.16 ÷ 30.026 = 6.00 → C₆H₁₂O₆. (d) 40.0% C; law of definite proportions (a pure compound has a fixed mass composition).
